questions.question: When chloroform is exposed to air and light, it is slowly oxidised to a highly poisonous gas. This gas is
options: Phosgene, $COCl_2$
Carbon tetrachloride, $CCl_4$
Chlorine, $Cl_2$
Carbon monoxide, $CO$

solution.key_concept: In the presence of air and light, chloroform is oxidised to phosgene.
steps: This is why chloroform must be protected from air and light during storage.
solution.why_not_others: $CCl_4$ is not formed by the oxidation of chloroform. $Cl_2$ is not produced, because the chlorine ends up in $COCl_2$ and $HCl$. $CO$ is not the product, because the carbon is converted to $COCl_2$.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that the poisonous product is $Cl_2$ or $CO$ simply because both are toxic gases.
solution.time_saving_tip: Chloroform plus air and light gives phosgene. Recall the oxidation directly.

questions.question: Chloroform is stored in closed, dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim, and about 1% ethanol is added to it. The ethanol is added
options: to lower the vapour pressure of chloroform so that it does not evaporate
to absorb light and prevent the photochemical oxidation of chloroform
to convert any phosgene formed into harmless ethyl carbonate
to oxidise chloroform completely to $CO_2$ and $HCl$

solution.key_concept: Ethanol acts as a scavenger that converts poisonous phosgene into a harmless compound.
steps: Some phosgene may still form despite the precautions taken during storage.
The added ethanol reacts with any phosgene present and converts it into harmless ethyl carbonate.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): to convert any phosgene formed into harmless ethyl carbonate
solution.why_not_others: Light is kept out by the dark-coloured bottle, not by ethanol. Air is excluded by filling the bottle to the brim. Ethanol does not oxidise chloroform, and its purpose is not to control evaporation.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the roles of the precautions: the dark bottle blocks light, filling to the brim removes air, and ethanol destroys phosgene.

questions.question: A single chlorine atom released from a freon in the stratosphere can destroy a very large number of ozone molecules. This is because, in the chain of reactions that destroys ozone, the species that is regenerated is
options: the $Cl\dot{O}$ radical
the $\dot{C}F_2Cl$ radical
the oxygen atom, $O$
the chlorine free radical, $\dot{C}l$

solution.key_concept: Ozone is destroyed by a chain reaction in which the chlorine radical is regenerated.
steps: In the first step, UV light splits the freon: $CF_2Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \dot{C}l + \dot{C}F_2Cl$.
The chlorine radical then attacks ozone: $\dot{C}l + O_3 \rightarrow Cl\dot{O} + O_2$.
The regenerated $\dot{C}l$ attacks another $O_3$ molecule, so the chain continues.
solution.why_not_others: $Cl\dot{O}$ is an intermediate that is consumed in the chain. $\dot{C}F_2Cl$ is formed only in the initiation step. The oxygen atom is consumed, not regenerated.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $Cl\dot{O}$ because it is a radical that appears during the chain.
solution.time_saving_tip: In a chain reaction, the species that both starts the chain and reappears at the end is the one that is regenerated.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: DDT gets stored in the fatty tissues of animals and its concentration builds up along food chains.
statements.R: Many species of insects have developed resistance to DDT.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: DDT biomagnifies because it is non-biodegradable and fat-soluble. Insect resistance is a separate problem.
steps: DDT is non-biodegradable and fat-soluble, so it is stored in fatty tissue and biomagnifies. A is true.
Many insects have indeed become resistant to DDT. R is true.
Insect resistance does not explain why DDT accumulates in fat. That is explained by its fat solubility and lack of biodegradability.
Therefore R is not the correct explanation of A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) is wrong because R does not explain A. Options (3) and (4) are wrong because both statements are true.
solution.common_trap: Linking any two true facts about DDT as cause and effect.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Iodoform acts as an antiseptic by virtue of the compound itself, and it was replaced by other formulations mainly because it is non-biodegradable.
statements.II: In the stratosphere, UV light splits $CF_2Cl_2$ to release a fluorine free radical, which then attacks ozone molecules.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Iodoform acts through liberated iodine and was discontinued because of its smell. Freons release chlorine radicals.
steps: The antiseptic action of iodoform is due to liberated iodine, not the compound itself.
Iodoform was replaced mainly because of its objectionable smell, so Statement I is incorrect.
The radical released is chlorine, not fluorine, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I gives the wrong mode of action and the wrong reason for discontinuing iodoform. Non-biodegradability is the problem with DDT. Statement II names the wrong radical, so no option that calls either statement correct can be right.
solution.common_trap: Believing that iodoform itself is the antiseptic, and assuming the radical released from a freon could be fluorine.
solution.time_saving_tip: The radical released from a freon always matches the halogen that destroys ozone, which is chlorine.
